name: Palace of Versailles
info: The Palace of Versailles is the château southwest of Paris that grew from Louis XIII's hunting lodge of 1623 into the residence of Louis XIV, Louis XV and Louis XVI, and the seat of the French court from 1682 to 1789.

facts.made: Begun as a hunting lodge for Louis XIII; expanded for Louis XIV by the architects Louis Le Vau, François d'Orbay and Jules Hardouin-Mansart, the painter Charles Le Brun and the garden designer André Le Nôtre, under the direction of Jean-Baptiste Colbert
facts.form: A château of courtyards and wings with a façade 402 metres long, about 63,154 square metres in area and roughly 2,300 rooms, set in a park of 815 hectares today, 93 of them formal gardens
facts.where: In the commune of Versailles in the Yvelines department, about 16 kilometres south-west of Paris; owned by the French state, and housing the National Museum of the History of France
facts.known: the Hall of Mirrors with its 578 mirrors; the State Apartments of the king and queen; the Royal Chapel and Royal Opera; the formal gardens of Le Nôtre; the Grand and Petit Trianon; the Queen's Hamlet; the court of Louis XIV; the treaties and proclamations signed there

t: Louis XIV turned his father's hunting lodge into a palace after seeing Nicolas Fouquet's Vaux-le-Vicomte in 1661, recruiting its architect, painter and garden designer, and the court lived at Versailles from 1682 until 6 October 1789.

Louis XIV made the palace the de facto capital of France by 1687, drawing the nobility there to seek prestige and royal patronage within a strict court etiquette, which eroded their provincial power bases.

The Revolution emptied the palace and sold its contents in seventeen thousand lots; Louis Philippe I made it a history museum, and restoration since 1892 has aimed to bring it back to its state in 1789.
dyk: Louis XIV's eight-foot-high silver throne in the Salon of Apollo was melted down in 1689 to help pay the costs of an expensive war, and was replaced by a more modest throne of gilded wood.
ev: Louis XIII built a modest brick-and-stone hunting lodge at Versailles
Louis XIV decided to make Versailles a full-scale residence and began encasing his father's château in Le Vau's enveloppe
The king, the court and the government settled at Versailles
The Women's March on Versailles forced the royal family to return to Paris, and the palace was closed
The Convention ordered the royal property in the palace sold at auction, a sale that ran until 1794
Louis Philippe I inaugurated the Museum of the History of France in the palace
The Treaty of Versailles, ending the First World War, was signed in the Hall of Mirrors
The Grand Versailles restoration project began with the replanting of the gardens

sections.origins:
The site of Versailles is first mentioned in 1038 in a charter of the Abbey of Saint-Père de Chartres. In the Middle Ages it held small villages, farmland and woodland, and in the 16th century the Gondi family, influential at court, owned the land. Louis XIII acquired part of it in 1623 and bought the remainder in 1632. In 1623 he built a modest brick-and-stone hunting lodge there, about 35 metres long, which contemporaries mocked as the "chétif château" ("puny château") and the "château de cartes" ("house of cards"). From 1631 to 1634 the architect Philibert Le Roy replaced the lodge with a château.

After Louis XIII died in 1643 his château was abandoned, and Anne of Austria, regent for the young Louis XIV, moved the court back to Paris. The Fronde, a series of revolts against royal authority from 1648 to 1653, left Louis XIV determined to rule alone. After Mazarin's death in 1661 he reformed his government to exclude his mother and the princes of the blood and ordered the expansion of his father's château into a palace. On 17 August 1661 he had been a guest at a festival given by Nicolas Fouquet at Vaux-le-Vicomte, where he saw the work of Louis Le Vau, André Le Nôtre and Charles Le Brun. He imprisoned Fouquet that September and recruited the three for his own projects.
sections.content:
The palace is a vast ensemble of courtyards and buildings designed to maintain architectural harmony. It covers about 63,154 square metres and has roughly 2,300 rooms. The eastern front is U-shaped, with the corps de logis and symmetrical advancing wings ending in the Dufour Pavilion to the south and the Gabriel Pavilion to the north, which enclose the Royal Court. Two larger asymmetrical wings flank it, giving a façade 402 metres long. The roofs cover about 10 hectares, and the palace has 2,143 windows, 1,252 chimneys and 67 staircases. Its earliest part, built for Louis XIII in brick, marble and slate, was surrounded in the 1660s by Le Vau's Enveloppe, inspired by Renaissance Italian villas.

The Hall of Mirrors, at the western end, is clad in marble and has 578 mirrors facing 17 windows. Le Brun's ceiling fresco shows the first 18 years of Louis XIV's reign in 30 scenes, 17 of them military victories over the Dutch. The Salon of War and the Salon of Peace stand at its northern and southern ends. The State Apartments of the king and queen occupied the main floor of the château neuf; the king's was an enfilade of seven rooms, each dedicated to a planet and its Roman god, reduced to five after the Hall of Mirrors was added. The Royal Chapel, 40 metres high, combines traditional Gothic royal church architecture with the French Baroque. The estate also holds the Grand Trianon, the Petit Trianon, the Queen's Hamlet and the gardens of Le Nôtre.
sections.making:
Work at first concentrated on the gardens. In 1668 and 1669, as the gardens grew and after the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1668), Louis XIV decided to turn Versailles into a full-scale royal residence. From 1668 to 1671 Le Vau encased Louis XIII's château on three sides in the enveloppe, which gave an Italianate façade over the gardens but kept the courtyard façade, a mix of styles that dismayed Louis XIV and that Colbert called a "patchwork". Jean-Baptiste Colbert managed the royal artisans and acted as intermediary with the king, who personally directed and inspected the planning and construction. Le Vau died in 1670, and his assistant François d'Orbay succeeded him at Versailles.

The Franco-Dutch War began in 1672 and funding was cut until 1674. After the war ended in a French victory in 1678, Jules Hardouin-Mansart became First Architect, with a restored budget and a large workforce of former soldiers. He added the Hall of Mirrors from 1678 to 1681, the Ministers' Wings, the stables, the Grand Commun and two new wings for the court. The Nine Years' War stopped work from 1688 until 1698, and the War of the Spanish Succession, with poor harvests in 1693–94 and 1709–10, led Louis XIV to cut funding and cancel planned work. The chapel was built from 1699 to 1710. The landscape was made from a bog using methods usually employed in fortress building, and water came from the damming of the river Bièvre in the 1660s and a pumping station on the Seine near Marly-le-Roi in 1681.
sections.reception:
Louis XIV used Versailles to promote himself, first with nighttime festivals in its gardens in 1664, 1668 and 1674, which print and engravings spread across Europe. From 1678 especially he sought to make it his seat of government. The court moved in 1682, though not officially, since opinion of Versailles was mixed among the nobility. By 1687 it was evident to all that Versailles was the de facto capital of France, and Louis XIV attracted the nobility there to seek prestige and royal patronage within a strict court etiquette, which eroded their traditional provincial power bases. He received the Doge of Genoa in 1685, an embassy from the Ayutthaya Kingdom in 1686 and one from Safavid Iran in 1715.

Court ceremony centred on the king's apartments, where the lever and the coucher, his waking up and going to bed, were attended by a crowd of courtiers, and at the Grand Couvert courtiers watched Louis XIV dine alone. After his death in 1715 the court left under the regency; the move broke the cultural power of Versailles, and under Louis XVI courtiers spent their leisure in Paris. The seven-year-old Mozart played there at Christmas 1763. The palace and its grounds had great influence on architecture and horticulture from the mid-17th century to the end of the 18th, seen in Christopher Wren's work at Hampton Court Palace, Berlin Palace, the Palace of La Granja, Stockholm Palace and Esterházy Palace, among others.
sections.survival:
The royal family left on 6 October 1789 after the Women's March on Versailles, and the palace was closed. In 1792 the National Convention ordered the paintings and sculptures sent to the Louvre, and in 1793 it ordered the royal property sold at auction. The sale ran from 25 August 1793 to 11 August 1794 and disposed of the furniture, mirrors, baths and kitchen equipment in seventeen thousand lots. Fleurs-de-lys and royal emblems were chiselled off the buildings, and in 1794 the Royal Gate was destroyed and the Cour de Marbre lost its floor. Napoleon considered making Versailles his residence but abandoned the idea because of the cost of renovation, and Louis XVIII ordered the royal apartments restored, but the task and cost were too great.

Louis Philippe I began the Museum of the History of France in 1833, inaugurated on 30 June 1837 and dedicated to "all the glories of France". To make it, practically all the apartments in the main building were demolished, with only the king's and queen's left almost intact. Restoration began in 1892 under the first conservator, Pierre de Nolhac, and John D. Rockefeller, Jr. gave $2,166,000 between 1925 and 1928. A bombing by Breton terrorists in 1978 heavily damaged parts of the palace. From the 1950s the aim was to restore the palace to its state in 1789, and the museum has spent considerable funds on original furnishings. The Grand Versailles project began in 2003, after Cyclone Lothar on 26 December 1999 had destroyed over 10,000 trees in the gardens, and the restoration of the Hall of Mirrors was completed in 2006.
sections.legacy:
The palace remained a stage for the state after the monarchy ended. During the Franco-Prussian War it was occupied by the German general staff, and the German Empire was proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors on 18 January 1871. In March 1871 the government of the Third Republic moved in, with the National Assembly meeting in the Opera, and the military operation that suppressed the Paris Commune was directed from Versailles. The Treaty of Versailles, ending the First World War, was signed in the Hall of Mirrors in June 1919. In 1783 the last two of the three treaties of the Peace of Paris, ending the American Revolutionary War, were signed at the palace.

Since the 1875 Constitution the Senate and National Assembly have met in joint session at Versailles to amend the French Constitution, as in 1999, 2000, 2003 and 2024. The palace is owned by the French state and since 1995 has been run as a Public Establishment supervised by the Ministry of Culture. The gardens of Le Nôtre became the epitome of the French formal garden style and were widely imitated. The palace is considered one of the masterpieces of French classical architecture, and it exerted major influence across Europe in the 18th and 19th centuries in architecture and the decorative arts.

summary: The Palace of Versailles grew from Louis XIII's hunting lodge of 1623 into the vast residence Louis XIV built, and the court lived there from 1682 to 1789. After the Revolution it became a history museum and a venue of state, and it has been restored since 1892.
notes: The article says the château was abandoned for 'the next decade' after 1643 and also that the estate fell into neglect for 'nearly two decades'; the profile says only that it was abandoned.

Start 1623 is the hunting lodge; the article also gives 1661 (expansion ordered) and 1664 (larger construction campaigns). Construction dates of the Hall of Mirrors vary in the article (1678 to 1681, 1678 to 1684, 1678 to 1686); 1678 to 1681 used.
The article gives the park as 815 hectares today and the estate as 800 hectares as of June 2021; the facts use 815.
